title: Circular Array Loop
statement:
The array `nums` holds non-zero integers and is treated as a ring: walking forward past the last index brings you to index `0`, and walking backward past index `0` brings you to the last index. Standing on index `i`, you jump `nums[i]` places forward when it is positive, or `|nums[i]|` places backward when it is negative.

Since every index has exactly one jump, following the jumps from any index eventually repeats. Return `true` if some cycle of these jumps exists that

- visits more than one distinct index (an index that jumps onto itself does not count), and
- uses only indices whose values all have the same sign (all forward jumps or all backward jumps).

Otherwise return `false`.
notes:
## Intuition

Each index has exactly one outgoing jump, so the array is a graph where every walk ends in a cycle. A simple approach walks from every index, finds the cycle it ends in and inspects it, which costs O(n²). Floyd's fast and slow pointers find a cycle on a walk in linear time. The extra trick is to stop a walk as soon as the direction changes, and to wipe out (set to 0) every index on a walk that failed, so no index is explored twice.

## Approach

1. Write `next(i)` as `i + nums[i]` wrapped into `[0, n)`; the double modulo handles negative jumps.
2. For each `start` not already wiped out, put `slow` and `fast` on it.
3. While `fast` and `next(fast)` have the same sign as `slow`, move `slow` one jump and `fast` two jumps.
4. If they meet, the walk has closed a loop with one direction. If the meeting index jumps onto itself, the loop is a self-loop and does not count; otherwise return `true`.
5. Otherwise no valid cycle can be reached from `start` along this direction, so set every index on that same-sign walk to `0`.
6. If every start fails, return `false`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [2, -1, 1, 2, 2]`, so `next` maps 0→2, 2→3, 3→0. From `start = 0`: after one round `slow = 2`, `fast = 3`; after two rounds `slow = 3`, `fast = 2`; after three rounds both are at `0`. All jumps on the way were forward, and `next(0) = 2 ≠ 0`, so the loop 0→2→3 has three indices: return `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each walk either returns or wipes the indices it explored, so every index is processed a constant number of times.
- Space: O(1): the input itself records which indices are finished.

## Pitfalls

- In JavaScript, Java and C, `%` keeps the sign of a negative left side; add `n` and take `%` again.
- A self-loop (`next(i) === i`, for example `nums[i]` a multiple of `n`) is a cycle of length 1 and must be rejected.
- Check the signs at both `fast` and `next(fast)` before each double jump, not only where `fast` lands; a loop that mixes directions must not count.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of the ring |
| `next` | index reached by jumping from `i` |
| `start` | index the current walk begins at |
| `slow`, `fast` | pointers that move one and two jumps per round |
| `sign` | direction of the failed walk, used while wiping it |
| `index`, `after` | the node being wiped and the one after it |
